chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Ismail ibn Abi al-Subbah, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

I asked him (peace be upon him) about the garment that one hands over to the fuller (bleacher), and he burns it. He (peace be upon him) said: 'He is liable (for the loss), for you only handed it over to him to repair it, and did not hand it over to him to spoil it.'

key_terms.أَغْرِمْهُ: He is liable / Make him pay compensation.
key_terms.الْقَصَّارِ: The fuller or bleacher, a type of artisan who cleans and prepares wool/cloth.

ai.seo_question: What is the legal ruling if a tailor or fuller destroys a customer's garment while working on it?
ai.summary: In *Al-Kafi*, Shaykh al-Kulayni records this narration from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) to establish the principle of *gharam* (financial liability) for artisans who damage entrusted goods. The Imam clarifies that the default contractual intent (*maqsid*) is repair and improvement; thus, destruction without cause constitutes a breach of trust, making the craftsman liable for compensation. This ruling underpins the Shia jurisprudence of *ithman* (liability) in commercial transactions.
